findings.explanation: The change replaces integer cent calculations with double dollar calculations and casts the result to int, truncating fractional cents. For example, a quantity of 1 now returns 12 instead of the correct 1250 cents, leading to incorrect total amounts.
Using (int)(PriceCatalog.unitPrice() * quantity) truncates the fractional cents, causing totalInCents to return an incorrect value for non‑whole‑cent prices.
The change from `>= 5000` to `> 5000` causes orders with a subtotal of exactly 5,000 cents to incorrectly incur a shipping fee of 500 cents instead of qualifying for free shipping.
The loop iterates one step beyond the array length, attempting to access values[values.length], which throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

The Checkout.totalInCents method now multiplies a double unit price by quantity and casts the result to int, truncating fractional cents. This causes incorrect total amounts for non‑whole‑cents prices.
The loop iterates one step beyond the array length, causing an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException when accessing values[i].

The change alters the free‑shipping threshold from subtotal >= 5000 to subtotal > 5000, causing orders with a subtotal of exactly 5000 cents to incorrectly incur a shipping fee of 500 cents instead of being free.
The loop reaches `values.length`, which is outside the array bounds, so every call with a non-null array throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` instead of returning the sum.
`unitPrice()` now returns dollars, but this calculation casts the dollar total directly to an integer without converting it to cents. For example, quantity 1 returns 12 instead of 1250.
The inclusive bound reaches `values[values.length]`, which is outside the array, so every call with a non-null array throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` instead of returning the sum.
The inclusive bound reaches `values[values.length]`, which is outside the array. As a result, `sum` throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` for every input, including an empty array.

The method still returns a total in cents, but `unitPrice()` is now expressed in dollars. Casting the dollar total to `int` truncates it without converting to cents, so a quantity of 1 returns 12 instead of 1250.
The inclusive condition runs one iteration past the last valid index, so every call eventually throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` instead of returning the sum (including for an empty array).
An order with a subtotal of exactly 5,000 cents now incurs a 500-cent shipping charge, despite qualifying for free shipping.
The loop includes `i == values.length`, so every call with a non-null array attempts to read past its last element and throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` instead of returning the sum.
`unitPrice()` now returns dollars, but this casts the dollar total directly to an integer instead of converting it to cents. For example, a quantity of 1 returns 12 instead of 1250.
The inclusive bound runs the loop once with `i == values.length`, so every call eventually reads past the end of the array and throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` instead of returning the sum.
A subtotal of exactly 5,000 cents now incurs a 500-cent fee, whereas the existing threshold made that subtotal eligible for free shipping.
